title: Psalm 146:1–10
context: First of the final Hallelujah doxologies that close the Psalter: Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD, my soul—while life and being last. Put your trust in princes, in a son of man with no salvation; when spirit departs, and he returns to earth and thoughts perish. Happy is he who has the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the LORD, his God—Maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all in them; who keeps truth forever; who executes justice for the oppressed, feeds the hungry, sets prisoners free, opens blind eyes, lifts the bowed down, loves the righteous, watches sojourners, upholds widow and fatherless, and ruins the wicked’s way. The LORD reigns forever, Zion’s God to all generations. Praise the LORD!

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Psalm 146:1–10.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English editions of the sources named.

arminian.quote: This is the first of the Psalms called Hallelujah Psalms, of which there are five, and which conclude the book. While I live will I praise—The true feeling of a heart overpowered with a sense of God’s goodness. While I have any being—in my continuance, in my progression, my eternal existence. Put not your trust in princes—God permitted change in a king’s disposition to teach the vanity of confidence in men, and the necessity of trusting in himself. His breath goeth forth—when he ceases to respire he ceases to live; all his thoughts, purposes, and projects come to nought and perish. Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the LORD his God—while he that trusts in man is miserable, he that trusts in God is happy. He made heaven and earth; he keeps his truth for ever; therefore his promises must be fulfilled to them that trust in him. The LORD shall reign for ever—therefore he can never fail; and he is thy God, O Zion. Therefore trust in him and bless the Lord.

reformed.quote: Trust not in princes: this admonition is appropriately inserted, for one means by which men blind themselves is involving their minds through inventions and being prevented from engaging in the praises of God. That God may have the whole praise due to him, David exposes and overthrows those false stays on which we would otherwise be too much disposed to trust. He names princes, from whom more is to be feared than common men—the great and wealthy have a dangerous attraction, suggesting that we take shelter under their patronage. The most powerful of the world’s princes is but a son of man—enough to rebuke our folly in worshipping them as a kind of demigods. Though princes are furnished with power, money, troops, and other resources, it is wrong to place our trust in frail mortal man. As soon as man has ceased to breathe, his corpse is subject to putrefaction; those who put their trust in men depend upon a fleeting breath; in that day all his thoughts perish. Blessed is he whose help is the Lord: the hopes of men are only stable and well-founded when they rest entirely upon God. He calls him the God of Jacob, to distinguish him from the multitude of false gods; it is only by an assured faith of adoption that any of us can rest upon him.
reformed.source: Commentary on the Book of Psalms (on Psalm 146)

verses.text: Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD, my soul.
verses.arminianNotes:
Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD, my soul! Clarke: first of the five closing Hallelujah Psalms.

Shared doxology: both camps begin where the finale begins—Hallelujah from the soul. Arminian readers answer the summons with willing praise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin’s concern is that God receive the whole praise due—false trusts steal doxology; Hallelujah restores it.

Praise undivided. Praise the LORD, my soul.

verses.text: While I live, I will praise the LORD. I will sing praises to my God as long as I exist.
verses.arminianNotes:
Praise as long as I live; sing while I have being. Clarke: heart overpowered with goodness; being as continuance.

Lifelong praise is sincerity’s length. Common confession: while I live; while I have being.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: praise to the end of the course—so God is not defrauded of ongoing thanks.

Perseverance in praise. Shared doxology across camps.

verses.text: Don’t put your trust in princes, in a son of man in whom there is no help.
verses.arminianNotes:
Put not trust in princes or a son of man—no salvation there. Clarke: vanity of confidence in men; necessity of trusting God.

Classical Arminians warn patrons and politics alike. Do not trust princes for salvation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: princes attract dangerous patronage; even the powerful are but a son of man—wrong to trust frail mortals as demigods.

Clear false stays so praise returns to God. Shared warning and shared cure: trust God, not princes.

verses.text: His spirit departs, and he returns to the earth. In that very day, his thoughts perish.
verses.arminianNotes:
Breath departs; returns to earth; plans perish that day. Wesley: as soon as dead; thoughts—designs for self or others perish.

Human schemes end with breath. Both readings hold: breath; earth; plans perish.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: trust in men depends on a fleeting breath; at that day thoughts flow away—ambitious plans vanish.

Mortality unmasks false hope. Shared anthropology: princes die; plans perish.

verses.text: Happy is he who has the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the LORD, his God,
verses.arminianNotes:
Blessed—help is the God of Jacob; hope in the LORD his God. Clarke: trust in man miserable; trust in God happy.

Both agree: this is the beatitude of the doxology. Classical Arminians plant hope in the LORD Himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: hopes stable only when entirely upon God; God of Jacob marks the true God versus false gods; rest by faith of adoption.

Blessed helper is Jacob’s God. Shared praise: blessed is he whose hope is in the LORD.

verses.text: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever;
verses.arminianNotes:
Maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all in them; keeps faith forever. Wesley: forever—He lives forever to fulfil promises and is eternally faithful.

Creator plus forever faithfulness grounds hope. Maker; keeps faith forever.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin’s blessed helper is no tribal mascot—He is Creator whose word stands. Forever faith underwrites praise.

The God who made all things is the one who keeps faith forever. Shared doxology: keeps faith forever.

verses.text: who executes justice for the oppressed; who gives food to the hungry. The LORD frees the prisoners.
verses.arminianNotes:
Justice for oppressed; food for hungry; sets prisoners free. Clarke: judgment for those who suffer violence or calumny; food; loosing captives.

Shared mercy agenda: both camps praise the LORD who rights, feeds, and frees. Classical Arminians urge hope here without camp-splitting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin clears false trusts so this God’s just, feeding, freeing character receives praise.

Praise for concrete mercies. Justice; food; prisoners free.

verses.text: The LORD opens the eyes of the blind. The LORD raises up those who are bowed down. The LORD loves the righteous.
verses.arminianNotes:
Opens blind eyes; lifts bowed down; loves the righteous. Clarke: opens eyes to wretchedness and salvation; raises the guilt-bowed; loves those in His image.

Sight, lifting, and love meet the needy and the righteous. The LORD opens blind eyes, lifts the bowed down, and loves the righteous.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin’s God of Jacob does what princes cannot sustain—sight, lifting, love of the righteous.

The LORD’s own verbs. Shared doxology across camps.

verses.text: The LORD preserves the foreigners. He upholds the fatherless and widow, but he turns the way of the wicked upside down.
verses.arminianNotes:
Watches sojourners; upholds widow and fatherless; ruins the wicked’s way. Clarke: preserves strangers; provides for widow/orphan; turns the wicked’s way upside down.

Agreed: tender toward vulnerable; opposed to wicked paths. Shared praise includes both sides of the verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin’s overthrow of false stays makes room to praise this holy care and holy ruin of wicked ways.

Watchfulness and judgment together. Sojourners; widow; fatherless; wicked ruined.

verses.text: The LORD will reign forever; your God, O Zion, to all generations. Praise the LORD!
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD reigns forever—Zion’s God to all generations. Praise the LORD! Clarke: He can never fail; trust Him and bless the Lord.

Shared finale: everlasting reign and Hallelujah. Classical Arminians and Reformed believers stand together in this closing doxology—no fork required.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin began by clearing rivals to praise; the psalm ends with forever reign and Hallelujah restored to God alone.

Zion’s God reigns forever. The LORD will reign forever. Praise the LORD!
